The White-tufted sunbeam (Aglaeactis castelnaudii) is a striking hummingbird endemic to the high-altitude puna grasslands of Peru, where it occupies an extreme environment characterized by intense solar radiation and large diurnal temperature fluctuations. At hatch, the altricial nestlings emerge at a remarkably small size, with an initial wet weight of just 0.9 grams [Ww0 = 0.9 grams], a value consistent with the tiny ova and minimal yolk reserves typical of trochilids. This initial weight is followed by a phase of rapid mass gain, as nestlings receive frequent provisions of nectar and small arthropods from the female. The embryonic development period, reflecting the time from egg fertilization to the first exogenous feeding event, has been documented under controlled incubation conditions. When maintained at a constant temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the incubation period lasts 17.5 days [ab = 17.5 days], a duration that aligns with the extended developmental schedules observed in many high-elevation Andean birds. This relatively protracted incubation likely reflects the metabolic constraints imposed by the cool thermal environment at altitude, where maintaining optimal egg temperatures requires substantial parental investment and brooding effort.

As the chicks progress through the nestling phase, their growth trajectory culminates in the attainment of adult body dimensions, though with pronounced sexual size dimorphism. Adult females of Aglaeactis castelnaudii achieve a maximum adult body mass of 6.2 grams [Wwi = 6.2 grams], whereas the males, which are typically the larger sex in this genus, reach a significantly higher ultimate wet weight of 7.2 grams [Wwi = 7.2 grams]. This degree of dimorphism is modest compared to some polygynous hummingbird species, but it likely reflects divergent selective pressures on the sexes; females invest heavily in egg production and incubation, while males engage in energetically costly territorial defense of flower patches. The fledging event, marking the first flight and nest departure, occurs relatively early in the developmental sequence. Under the typical active metabolic body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]—a temperature maintained by the incubation of the eggs and the brooding of the nestlings—the time since birth at fledging is 22 days [tx = 22 days]. This rapid transition to flight capability is an adaptation that minimizes the period of high nest vulnerability to predation.

Sexual maturation in the White-tufted sunbeam follows a predictable developmental schedule, with the onset of puberty representing a key life-history transition. At the same core body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] that characterizes the active metabolic phase, the time since birth at puberty is 66 days [tp = 66 days]. This rapid attainment of reproductive maturity, occurring just a few months after fledging, is among the fastest recorded for a hummingbird of this body size and is likely an adaptation to the brief austral summer breeding window available at high elevations. The physiological activation of the gonads, marked by a surge in testosterone in males and follicular development in females, enables young birds to enter the breeding population within the same season they were hatched. However, despite this early physiological readiness, first reproduction is typically deferred until the following breeding season due to the demanding energetic costs of establishing a territory and the need to accumulate sufficient body condition. This temporal lag between puberty and first breeding creates an important distinction in the species' life-history calendar.

The timing of the first reproductive event itself, representing the age at first successful brood, is a critical demographic parameter. Field observations and mark-recapture studies indicate that the age at first brood is 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], coinciding with the onset of the next breeding season following a hatchling's first winter at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This delay, measured under the maintenance body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] that supports active foraging and metabolism, reflects the time required for subadult birds to acquire a feeding territory, learn effective foraging strategies on the challenging puna landscape, and accumulate sufficient lipid reserves to sustain the high energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The reproductive strategy itself is characterized by low annual fecundity. Females produce only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], a rate consistent with the k-selected life-history strategies common to many high-altitude tropical birds. Within this single annual breeding event, the clutch size is strictly two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], a remarkably consistent constraint that likely reflects both the limited brood-patch space of the small female and the energetic limitations of provisioning two rapidly growing altricial chicks in a resource-scarce environment.

Longevity and metabolic rate are fundamental to understanding the energetic economy of this species. The maximum recorded lifespan for Aglaeactis castelnaudii in the wild, based on long-term banding studies, is approximately 2665 days [am = approximately 2665 days], a value measured in individuals operating at their active body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This lifespan is relatively modest for a hummingbird, with some congeners in less extreme environments living substantially longer, likely due to the elevated metabolic demands and high predation risks characteristic of the puna zone. The metabolic underpinnings of this energetic lifestyle are reflected in the basal metabolic rate, which represents the minimum energetic cost of maintaining vital physiological processes. Respirometry trials conducted on post-absorptive, resting individuals at thermoneutrality revealed a basal oxygen consumption of 18.18 milliliters per hour [JOi = 18.18 milliliters per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This value is particularly notable given the bird's small body mass, as it represents a mass-specific metabolic rate that is among the highest recorded for any endotherm. This elevated metabolism is a direct adaptation to the cold, oxygen-thin high-altitude environment, permitting the sustained hovering flight and high foraging activity necessary to meet daily energetic demands in a habitat where floral nectar resources are patchy and seasonally variable.
